prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Context: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) NextGen improves National Airspace System (NAS) capacity/efficiency. National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Airspace Technology Demonstrations 3 (ATD-3) integrates ground/aircraft aids for weather avoidance, Traffic Management Initiatives (TMIs), and en route/arrival metering.
Elements/actors: FAA traffic managers; air traffic control system/controllers; aircraft; aircraft/flight operators; airline flight dispatchers; pilots/flight crews; public; NASA; industry; air traffic management (ATM) stakeholders; flight management systems; onboard weather radar.
Operations: TMIs divert/meter aircraft for safe separation. Managers designate forecast-convection Flow Constrained Areas (FCAs). Severe Weather Avoidance Plans (SWAP), alias Playbook routes, address constraints 2–8 hours ahead. Dispatchers must file plans ≥45 minutes before gate push-back and select/revise SWAP routes. Collaborative Trajectory Options Program (CTOP) receives operator route options/departure-delay preferences; no postdeparture optimization. Crews coordinate alternate trajectories with controllers/dispatchers and must coordinate conflict avoidance with controllers.
Dynamic Weather Routes (DWR): NASA ground-based trajectory automation, extending Direct-To (1998–2001), continuously analyzes flights at/above 10,000 ft, updating trajectories from received radar tracks/flight plans and weather/airspace/traffic data. It seeks simple wind-corrected time/fuel-saving amendments considering convection, traffic, sector congestion, special use airspace and FAA restrictions. Programmable Maneuver Start Point (MSP) defaults to five minutes downstream or first high-altitude-airspace point. Default Return Capture Fix (RCF), a downstream current-plan waypoint, approximates acceptable clearance considering location, routing, local airspace and destination arrival limits. Reference direct route MSP–RCF must meet user minimum savings (default five minutes), then undergo weather/traffic probing. Weather conflicts trigger one/two auxiliary waypoints seeking minimum delay; optional automatic MSP/waypoint adjustment integrates weather/traffic resolution. Qualifying solutions post route advisories to user-display alert lists. Users inspect/modify before requesting/issuing clearance; interface strongly warns of modified-route forecast-weather/traffic conflicts. Direct-To advisories need no convection. Polygon avoidance supports nonweather obstacles. FAA implementation unspecified. Conditions: fair/adverse weather, SWAP active; no formal modes.

New part:
U0064: Figure 1: DWR Concept Overview Inserted auxiliary waypoints are initially computed using fix-radial-distance points which may be placed anywhere for a minimum delay solution.
U0065: A snap-to named fix option automatically replaces any auxiliary waypoints with nearby named fixes for ease of use in voice-based operations.
U0066: Snap-To solutions that avoid weather, or optionally weather and traffic, are posted to the DWR alert list if they meet the minimum flight-time savings criteria.
U0067: The current flight plan trajectory and the DWR-advised trajectory are both analyzed for conflict with congested airspace sectors and with Special Use Airspace (SUA).
U0068: The traffic congestion and SUA status are incorporated into the user interface display so the user may consider these factors when evaluating the DWR route advisory.
U0069: By clicking the DWR advisory the user activates an automated interactive trial planning function to visualize the route and if necessary modify the RCF, the MSP, and any inserted auxiliary waypoints.
U0070: Flight-time savings and weather and traffic conflicts status update rapidly (within 1 sec) and automatically as the user modifies the DWR route.
U0071: Figure 2: DWR Automation Process The RCF is a downstream fix on the current Center route of flight at which the DWR route correction rejoins the original flight plan trajectory.
U0072: A limit function unique to the particular airspace region (i.e., unique to each Center’s airspace) determines the default RCF to be used for DWR route correction computations.
U0073: The purpose of the limit function is to define a default RCF for any flight given its present position and current route of flight such that a direct route from present aircraft track position to the RCF is generally operationally acceptable if weather were not a factor.
U0074: The RCF is a function of Center airspace and arrival routing limits, and may be a function of other factors such as the particular routing (city pair routing for example) in the given Center airspace and the first-tier adjacent Center airspace.
U0075: The RCF is generally not the last fix within the Center boundary where the aircraft is currently located.
U0076: The NASA DWR automation for Fort Worth Center employs a limit rectangle that extends roughly 200 nmi beyond the ZFW boundary (see Figure 3).

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.
